# Let the compiler read the geometry

[Predict the coordinates before you run the code.]{.lesson-deck}
:::

An origin and a spacing are both triples of real numbers, but swapping
them changes the physics. OpenPFC gives them separate types so the function
signature can express what each triple means.

## Put meaning into the arguments

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="arguments"}
```

The first assertion verifies the intended call. The second verifies that
the compiler rejects the same arguments with origin and spacing exchanged.
This is a small compile-time check of an API property, not an intentional
build failure hidden in a comment.

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="construct" dedent=2}
```

The grid has 64 samples. Its fully periodic extent is $(2,4,4)$, so its
geometric centre is $(0,0,2)$. That centre is a point in physical space;
it need not coincide with a stored sample on an arbitrary grid.

## Change the geometry confidently

```sh
openpfc run model.cpp input.json --launcher=none
```

The empty input is unused; this lesson invites edits to the C++ expression.
Change the origin and predict the centre's translation. Change the spacing
and predict the extent. The runtime check verifies the concrete count and
centre, while the static assertions verify the argument-order property.

These wrappers distinguish roles, not physical units. `GridSpacing` does
not know whether a number is in metres or micrometres, and a correctly typed
value can still describe the wrong experiment. Use consistent units in the
model equations and inputs. See the
[strong type definitions](https://github.com/VTT-ProperTune/OpenPFC/blob/master/include/openpfc/kernel/data/strong_types.hpp)
and continue with [anisotropic coordinates](../anisotropic-grid/index.qmd).

The complete [C++ model](model.cpp) and [starting input](input.json)
are available with this lesson.

:::
